# Local periodic families survive a nonelliptic perturbation

The literal statement specifies a nonconstant smooth family of periodic phase points. It does not require the family to extend around an entire invariant circle. Under that definition, all distinct pairs $p,q\ge2$ are realizable for inner billiards; for outer billiards all distinct pairs $p,q\ge3$ are realizable. Outer period two is impossible. These are local-family constructions, not a solution of a stronger porism or global constant-width version of the historical question.

Here is one construction that simultaneously works for any prescribed finite list of admissible periods. Start with the unit circle. For an inner period $r\ge3$, take its regular inscribed $r$-gon, traversed in cyclic order once; for$r=2$ take a diameter traversed back and forth. Rotating the polygon by an angle$\theta$ in a small open interval gives a smooth family of billiard phase points. The reflection law holds because the two incident regular-polygon chords make equal angles with the circle tangent. For$r=2$ the incidence is normal. Its least period is exactly$r$: before$r$ reflections the boundary point has not returned. The parameter changes the initial boundary point, so this is not a reparameterization of one finite orbit.

For each prescribed period collect every contact point of one starting polygon. This is a finite set of circle angles. Choose sufficiently short neighborhoods of those distinct angles whose union is not the whole circle. By restricting the rotation interval, every contact point of every member of every chosen family remains inside this union$U$. Choose a nonnegative nonzero smooth periodic bump$b$ supported in a nonempty complementary open interval. Replace the circle by the radial curve
\[
\gamma_\varepsilon(\phi)=(1+\varepsilon b(\phi))(\cos\phi,\sin\phi).
\]
For sufficiently small$\varepsilon>0$, this is embedded and has everywhere positive curvature. Indeed its curvature numerator is$r^2+2(r')^2-rr''$, which converges uniformly to one as$\varepsilon\to0$; its radius is positive. The enclosed body$K_\varepsilon$ contains the unit disk, and its boundary and tangent agree exactly with the circle on$U$. The selected inner polygon chords remain in$K_\varepsilon$, with the same reflection law at all their vertices. Thus every selected inner family survives unchanged.

The curve is not an ellipse. It agrees with the unit circle on a nonempty open arc, yet differs elsewhere. If a quadratic equation defining an ellipse vanished on an open circle arc, substituting$(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$ would give a trigonometric polynomial vanishing on an interval, hence identically. Its zero ellipse would therefore be the circle. This contradicts the nonzero bump.

For the outer construction fix$r\ge3$, set$\alpha=\pi/r$, and take vertices
\[
x_j=\sec\alpha\,(\cos(\theta+2j\alpha),\sin(\theta+2j\alpha)).
\]
Their edge midpoints$t_j=(x_j+x_{j+1})/2$ lie on the unit circle, since their distance from the origin is$\sec\alpha\cos\alpha=1$. Each edge is tangent to the circle at$t_j$, and$x_{j+1}=2t_j-x_j$. Choose the cyclic direction consistent with the prescribed side in the definition of$T$. This is an outer orbit of least period$r$, as its$r$ vertices are distinct. Rotate through a small interval and preserve all contact arcs$t_j$ by the same bump construction, now using these angles when defining$U$.

A tangent line at an unchanged contact of a strictly convex body is globally supporting; its only boundary contact is that point. Consequently its two selected exterior vertices, which lie on the tangent line away from$t_j$, remain outside$K_\varepsilon$, and the prescribed-side tangent remains the one used by$T$. Every orbit and its primitive period survives. The initial exterior point varies with$\theta$, so these again are nonconstant phase-point families.

Finally, no outer two-cycle exists for any strictly convex table with the stated side convention. If$T(x)=y$ and$T(y)=x$, their contact points both equal$(x+y)/2$. On this same supporting line the two vectors pointing from$x$ and$y$ to the contact have opposite directions. The body lies on opposite sides relative to these oriented vectors, so only one can satisfy the prescribed side. This is a contradiction. Fixed points are also excluded because$x=t$ is not exterior.

The construction imposes no analyticity and relies essentially on smooth local modifications. It establishes existence for the literal period-pair question; it neither classifies all tables admitting these families nor supplies full closed invariant curves. Tabachnikov's original discussion emphasizes constant-width families and motivates that stronger setting. Keeping the local/global distinction is necessary to avoid claiming that this perturbation resolves that historical rigidity problem.
